title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is explaining Lagrange's method for integrating dx/√X ± dy/√Y = 0, where X = A+Bx+Cx²+Dx³+Ex⁴ and Y is the same quartic in y. The method yields Euler's algebraic addition theorem in symmetric form:

F(x,y) := [2A + B(x+y) + 2Cxy + Dxy(x+y) + 2Ex²y² ∓ 2√(XY)]/(x−y)² = Δ (constant).

In §56 Euler takes X to be a perfect square, √X = R = a+bx+cx², √Y = S = a+by+cy², so that A=a², B=2ab, C=b²+2ac, D=2bc, E=c². For the difference equation dx/R − dy/S = 0, the +2RS version of F reduces to (a + ½b(x+y) + cxy)²/(x−y)² = const. Taking the square root gives the bilinear integral of Theorem I.

§57: for the sum equation dx/R + dy/S = 0 the relevant form carries −2RS. Expanding,
2RS = 2a² + 2ab(x+y) + 2ac(x²+y²) + 2b²xy + 2bcxy(x+y) + 2c²x²y².
The numerator therefore becomes 4acxy − 2ac(x²+y²) = −2ac(x−y)². So F ≡ −2ac identically. The 'integral' is the tautology Δ = −2ac and says nothing about the solution curves.

§58 states this as an 'Insigne Paradoxon': a correctly derived general integral becomes void exactly when X and Y are squares. The task is to explain this and to recover the true integral. The true integral exists and is algebraic: ∫dx/R is (up to a factor) log((x−r₁)/(x−r₂)), so the integral is a symmetric (1,1)-relation.

§59 (continued on the next page): this is not the familiar 0/0 or ∞−∞ indeterminacy. Euler resolves it by perturbation, setting X = R²+α and Y = S²+α with α infinitesimal. He expands √X = R + α/2R and extracts the nontrivial information at first order in α. In modern terms: when a one-parameter family of first integrals degenerates to a constant at a parameter value, the first α-derivative, i.e. the limit of (F_α − F_0)/α, is a genuine first integral.
errors: No mathematical error on this page: Δ = −2ac checks out exactly, since the numerator minus 2RS equals −2ac(x−y)².
Minor imprecision: Euler calls the equation 'absurd'. It is not contradictory, it is an identity (trivially true), so it is void rather than false.

ideas.what: Degenerate case of Euler's symmetric biquadratic addition-theorem integral when the quartic X is a perfect square: the first integral collapses to the constant −2ac.
ideas.modern_name: Degeneration of the elliptic addition law to the genus-0 (rational/logarithmic) case; trivial first integral at a degenerate parameter
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (addition theorem); degenerations are a standard later topic
ideas.where_published: E506 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petropol. 1780, publ. 1784; Opera Omnia I.21 – volume unsure)

ideas.what: Resolving the vanishing of a first integral by perturbing the parameter (X = R²+α) and taking the first-order coefficient in α.
ideas.modern_name: Differentiating a family of first integrals with respect to a parameter; limiting process in degenerate families
ideas.usually_credited_to: General folklore of perturbation/limits; Euler uses analogous limit tricks elsewhere

ideas.what: Euler's explicit remark that this indeterminacy is of a new kind, neither 0/0 nor ∞−∞, and unprecedented in his experience.

missed.claim: The paradox is in effect the genus drop of the curve w² = X(x) when X becomes a square (elliptic → rational). Euler's perturbation X = R²+α is the first-order deformation off the degenerate (nodal) fibre. The page anticipates the idea that integrals of degenerate fibres are recovered as derivatives of the general family. Whether historians have framed it this way is unsure, but it is a modest, rather natural observation.
missed.quote: quaeritur enodatio huius insignis difficultatis ac praecipue modus, hinc verum integralis valorem investigandi
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly of historiographic interest, as an early instance of deformation and limiting arguments for degenerating elliptic integrals. It has no new mathematical content today.

deep.surprise_reason: The computation is correct and the paradox and its resolution are in a published, known paper. The conceptual point (a first integral degenerating to a constant, cured by a perturbation in the parameter) is neat but well within standard technique. It is probably noted in the Opera Omnia commentary, though I am unsure.
